item.title: I pulled the mainboard out of my Framework Laptop 13 and turned it into a truly modular Proxmox server
item.itunes:title: I pulled the mainboard out of my Framework Laptop 13 and turned it into a truly modular Proxmox server
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Framework makes some solid laptops that are excellent if you're all about serviceability. Being able to take apart your laptop and actually make meaningful changes to it is nothing short of liberating. If my Framework Laptop 13 happens to suffer a hardware fault, I can order a new part straight from the manufacturer with zero fuss. I take the laptop apart, remove the old component, and install the replacement, and we're once again up and running. But I thought, "How about taking that modularity to the home lab?"

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Why use a Framework Laptop mainboard as a home server?

What would prompt someone to use a laptop in the home lab?

There's a reason why so many appreciate the low-power capabilities of a mini PC. Sure, a used enterprise server in a 5U chassis looks the part and certainly makes one believe they're running a home-based data center, but it's not quite as simple as that. These old servers usually have less efficient parts because data centers aren't particularly fussed when it comes to power draw. No one is sitting in the same room as the server for hours on end.

Even 1U servers with seemingly efficient Intel Xeon chips can pump out a lot of heat and noise. Those fans spin fast and take a fair amount of power to handle the load placed on the server with self-hosting and then some. That's why people opt to consolidate from enterprise gear or switch things up and go with small form-factor systems and mini PCs. I went with the latter to begin with. A single Threadripper 9980X undervolted sounded like a great idea to run the entire home lab, replacing three 1U servers.

Turn out, it's not saving me any power at all. Parts are just as expensive for workstations such as the AMD Threadripper platform. Granted, components are more readily available and standard, but this is what led me to a mini PC doing the job. It takes a fraction of the power input and yet manages to achieve some reasonable results. The same goes for a Framework Laptop mainboard, which is essentially just a fancy mini PC that fits inside a laptop chassis. Framework even sells a desktop chassis for the board.

The Laptop 13 I have at hand generally pulls anywhere between 5 and 8 watts at idle running Arch Linux. Running as a headless server, I would hazard a guess it would be even lower. That's quite the baseline and a much more manageable amount than 120W or so with the Threadripper server build. When pushed hard, one can see around 30 watts pulled from the power brick, but even that's a substantial saving compared to used servers and workstation consolidation projects.

I spent less than $150 to build a Proxmox home server with an SBC

No, it's not the Raspberry Pi

5
By  Ayush Pande

Transforming the laptop into a home server

Who needs a chassis to protect internal components?

The first port of call was to extract the mainboard from the Laptop 13. This isn't terribly challenging at all, and Framework has some excellent guides available in true iFixit fashion if you get stuck along the way. Once disconnected from the keyboard, screen, battery, and then some, we have a simple yet capable single-board computer (SBC). Everything is present and ready to roll. The CPU, GPU, RAM, and storage are all soldered or installed on the primary PCB, so once removed, a single USB-C power input will see this thing boot up.

Framework even includes a dedicated power switch on the PCB. If you have a 3D printer at hand, it would be possible to create some extravagant case for this thing, incorporating a means to boot it up into the design. With the mainboard powered on, I booted into my favorite multi-OS tool to select Proxmox and start the familiar home server installation process. 16 GB of DDR5 RAM is presently installed, which is ample for running a few services. (If you have a gold mine, more can be added.)

The AMD Ryzen 7 7840U is a decent enough CPU with plenty of power on tap. It has eight physical cores with 16 threads available for various processes. It won't win any awards for the mightiest workstation or gaming chip, but it will be perfect for running some Linux containers (LXCs) and virtual machines (VMs). A total of 96GB is supported, which would put this right up there with some of the best platforms for running Proxmox and some services.

Thermal performance is actually rather brilliant, thanks to not being enclosed inside a tightly packed package with other components producing heat. Having plenty of space around the SBC makes it possible to enjoy better sustained performance under load compared to the laptop form factor, though the Framework 13 is certainly no slouch. It's just that AMD's Ryzen chips simply don't come close to Snapdragon in terms of efficiency.

I turned a nearly 10-year-old laptop into the most useful machine in my home lab

I can't imagine my home lab without it

3
By  Ayush Pande

Should everyone do this?

No. I don't recommend you go and buy a Framework Laptop 13 or even just the mainboards and use them as a home server. Actually, I do if you can source one at a steep enough discount, but for most people, used PC parts, a mini PC, or some other form factor would be a better option. If you do, however, have a spare Framework laptop at hand or fancy yourself a small project on the side, it's quite the compelling setup, being able to extract the board and power it up like it's an SBC.

Framework Laptop 13
Operating System
None, Windows 11 Home, Windows 11 Pro
CPU
Intel 13th-gen P-series, AMD Ryzen 7040 series
GPU
Intel UHD or Iris Xe graphics, Radeon 700M Graphics
Storage
Up to 4TB PCIe 4.0 SSD
Battery
55Wh or 61Wh
Display (Size, Resolution)
13.5-inch IPS 3:2, 2256x1504 resolution, 100% sRGB, 400 nits

The Framework Laptop 13 is one of the most modular laptops you can buy in 2023. You can swap out all the components right down to the mainboard. New on this year's model is the option for 13th-generation Intel CPUs, along with AMD Ryzen processors for the first time. 

$849 at Framework

item.title: The JBL Vibe Beam 2 earbuds become budget-friendly at just $40
item.itunes:title: The JBL Vibe Beam 2 earbuds become budget-friendly at just $40
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A good pair of earbuds can go a long way, especially if you're someone who relies on public transit. You could go all out with something like Apple's AirPods or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but those cost a fortune. Instead, we recommend grabbing a pricey pair that's steeply discounted, like the JBL Vibe Beam 2. Right now, you can save 38% on Amazon, taking the price from $65 to $40. While the former price isn't bad, we'll take the latter one any day of the week.

Tons of value at its current price

You get solid audio, which can be customized to your liking thanks to an EQ, along with good ANC, and the battery life can stretch to 40 hours with the included charging case.

That's 10 hours with the earbuds alone, and an additional 30 hours of charging with the case. It also has four microphones for crisp voice quality during calls. These earbuds will allow to connect and switch between eight devices at once.

The earbuds also feature an IP54 rating, which means they can withstand some moisture and dust, making them perfect for the gym or if you get caught in bad weather.

If this all sounds interesting, you can pick up the JBL Vibe Beam 2 earbuds in four different colors from Amazon at the discount price of $40. We've read through some of the reviews on Amazon and most customers come away happy. And at the $40 price, you're getting a lot of value here.

JBL has been making audio products for some time, and we think that the Vibe Beam 2 will be to your liking.

item.title: I let Claude Code debloat my 4-year-old Windows laptop, and it found 30 GB of junk I never needed
item.itunes:title: I let Claude Code debloat my 4-year-old Windows laptop, and it found 30 GB of junk I never needed
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As a part of my job, I run various experiments on both of the machines I have at home, which includes my main desktop and a 2022 Lenovo Legion 5 Pro, which means that my SSDs fill up with leftover installers, packages, and files that I use once and never look at again. I've had my fair share of experience with both free and paid debloating tools, but making them work often means working alongside them. More often than not, they'd clean up a few gigabytes and then leave me chasing utilities I'd absent-mindedly deleted in bulk.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So, I found myself wondering if I could build a debloating solution tailored to my laptop, which would exclude the files I might still want and look in places on my drive that generic debloaters could never reach. With that in mind, I handed the job to Claude Sonnet 5.5 through Claude Code, and it found 30GB of junk that I could get rid of in just three minutes. So far, it has worked better than any other cleanup utility I've ever used.

I started with a storage audit with a free utility

WizTree makes it easy to visualize your bloat

Before jumping into PowerShell with Claude, I wanted to take a cursory glance at my drive and check every recommendation it would make against the numbers I'd tallied myself. To do this, I fired up WizTree, which is a free disk space analyzer that reads the NTFS Master File Table directly and scans an entire drive in a matter of seconds when run with admin privileges.

I found a rather cluttered, disorganized drive after the run, just as I had expected from a laptop that hadn't seen any deliberate signs of maintenance since 2022. About 213GB of the C: drive was in use, and the treemap the utility uses for representation made some of the worst offenders visible from a mile away. My C:\Users folder alone accounted for over 110GB, and the Recycle Bin had been holding 20GB of files I had "deleted" but forgotten to empty from the bin.

The device itself had telltale signs of a hamfisted job of maintenance, with a C:\Temp folder that hadn't been touched since June 2022, and a 3GB Drivers folder from the factory install. Certainly, Claude had plenty to work with. I exported the full scan as a CSV file and saved a text document detailing every installed app before handing off to Sonnet 5.5, which gave me a baseline for future reference and let me see whether Opus could discover this hidden mess on its own.

I made Claude Code build a map of my files, and it cut search times by 96%

My files are still a mess, but at least Claude knows where they are

2
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Then, I let Claude Sonnet 5.5 work its magic

It took one prompt, and my wish was its command

The prompt I delivered was as simple as it could get, but I deliberately added certain exclusions to err on the side of caution with this run.

"Debloat this 4-year-old Legion 5 Pro (running Windows 11 26H2). Find any junk files, caches, leftover installers, bloatware (both by the OEM and Microsoft) along with unneeded startup items. First, audit the files only. Change nothing, and give me a table of everything you would remove, along with its size and how safe it is to remove. Remove only the items I approve, and log each one with the space freed to debloat-log.md in this folder. Don't touch anything in OneDrive, System Volume Information, Recovery, Dev Drive, C:\Llama.cpp, C:\Games, Models folders, .ckpt files, or the Recycle Bin."

As you can imagine, everything that I had excluded had a reason for doing so. OneDrive was obvious, since anything that's deleted here also disappears from the cloud copy. As for System Volume Information, it had to be protected as it holds the restore point I created before the run, acting as a safety net on the off-chance something went wrong. The Recovery folder on the other hand, holds the environment that Reset this PC and Startup repair rely on.

Everything else that I had excluded, I did to protect my work on the PC. The Dev Drive is a 15GB virtual disk I use for testing, and Llama.cpp, my games folder, my model folders, and my .ckpt checkpoint files are all the test materials I routinely need. Also worth noting that before the test, I changed the permission mode in Claude Code from auto to manual, since Claude Code now starts in auto mode by default. This ensured that every file I deleted waited for my sign-off beforehand.

My C: drive kept running out of space, and I finally found how to stop it for good

I had to modify certain habits to keep my C: drive breathing

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Claude Code found 30GB of junk in three minutes

Some of it had been sitting there since the day I unboxed it

At medium effort, Sonnet 5.5 took about three minutes and twenty-three seconds to return a tiered list of junk files, bloatware, leftover installers and other startup items ranked by how safe they were to remove, at which point, I knew that it was a strong result already. I took a careful look through the categorized items, and found that junk and caches added up to about 8GB, whereas old installers and files came at 14GB. The apps Opus recommended for removal came to another 8GB.

The oldest of finds had been there since day one of purchasing the laptop. C:\Drivers as it turns out, was Lenovo's factory driver dump from 2021, and it had company in the form of the Lenovo Companion app, a McAfee out-of-the-box upgrade task (which I'm surprised was a thing even in 2021) and Microsoft's usual suspects, with Clipchamp, Disney+, and Solitaire leading a list of 23 stock apps that I never once opened in my life.

The rest, however, were my own doing. I discovered a ReasonLabs antivirus that I probably installed at some point and had forgotten long back, which had seven services set up right alongside Windows Defender.

The other embarrassing items taking up space on the drive included Lavasoft's Web Companion, and a 4.5GB PanFone recovery folder from my iPhone 7 days in the C:\temp folder, which I assume I needed to fix a boot loop and get out of the DFU mode. Regardless, everything from that phone has long been backed up to iCloud, so the folder had no reason to stay. Claude also flagged a 4.5GB Nvidia shader cache, and since I no longer game on this laptop, that one may as well be three years old as well.

An unexpected use-case for my $20 subscription?

One of the things that most debloaters miss is the intelligence of a frontier model and its ability to recall training data to recognize what belongs on your PC versus what doesn't. In my experience, it has been entirely worth spending some of my tokens on a task that took just a little over three minutes and spared me hours of jumping from one folder to another. If you follow a similar approach, it's worth keeping in mind the safeguards I deployed that would help Claude easily separate the junk from the files that you may one day need.

item.title: Every show on my media server gets subtitles automatically now, and I haven't searched for one in months
item.itunes:title: Every show on my media server gets subtitles automatically now, and I haven't searched for one in months
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
After a full year of self-hosting, jumping between Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby before finally selecting Jellyfin, I absolutely love having a self-hosted media server. However, there's one piece of the puzzle I've never managed to get right, and I'm sure millions of users will agree with me on this: subtitles.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

If I had a dollar for how many times I've had my immersion broken midway through an episode or movie before opening a separate website and hunting down a subtitle file, I'd be halfway to paying for the Lifetime Plex Pass. Jellyfin offers a solution with a plugin, but my experience with it has been less than stellar.

So I finally stopped hunting for subtitles manually and looked for a way to automate the whole process. In doing so, I've fundamentally changed how I maintain my media library.

Jellyfin’s built-in subtitle fetching was never going to cut it

Finding the right subtitle every time isn't easy

Nothing is more frustrating than having to pause something on Jellyfin just because the subtitles are missing. Jellyfin lets you fetch subtitles manually, but that interrupts playback and forces you through plenty of menus. In the end, you still have to hope the downloaded subtitle file matches your release. Nothing quite kills the momentum of a good show like playing subtitle roulette.

Naturally, the first solution most Jellyfin users reach for is the OpenSubtitles plugin. It's perfectly serviceable for grabbing an occasional subtitle, and I have nothing against it as a manual tool. In fact, it's practically frictionless, since it's an official plugin that you simply have to enable. However, you can't expect it to maintain an entire library without your intervention.

Jellyfin's scheduled subtitle downloads are surprisingly opaque, offering little visibility into what it fetches, which providers it queries, or why certain episodes remain untouched. That's because downloading one subtitle and maintaining subtitles across an entire media library are two very different problems. I needed something considerably more dependable.

Bazarr's unconventional approach helped me out

The tool that fixes Jellyfin's subtitles never actually talks to it

Bazarr, the application that finally solved my subtitle woes, doesn't actually integrate with Jellyfin at all. In fact, it doesn't even scan my media folders on its own. Instead, it relies on Sonarr and Radarr to keep track of your TV shows and movies, respectively, and then uses that information to find matching subtitles.

Once Bazarr finds a suitable match, it simply downoads the subtitle file alongside the video, usually as an SRT sidecar file. Jellyfin then detects the file during its regular library scans and makes it available for playback. This entire process doesn't require any plugins, API integrations, or special Jellyfin configuration.

At first, I scoffed at the idea of a subtitle provider that never even talked to my media server. However, I've realized that it's actually a rather clever design choice. Since Bazarr operates at the filesystem level, it doesn't care which media server you use. Jellyfin, Plex, and Emby can all benefit from the same subtitle automation without dedicated integrations.

I used local AI to fix bad subtitles in my media library

I let local AI rewrite the bad subtitles in my media library, and I'll never go back.

By  Dhruv Bhutani

There is, however, one small catch. To get Bazarr running, you must also have Sonarr and Radarr running. These are both TV show and movie managers, and Bazarr connects to the media library on your PC through them. That's three applications instead of one, but the resulting architecture is considerably more flexible than another media-server-specific plugin.

My subtitle pipeline is now pretty hands-off

The real magic happens after you've finished configuring everything

A single Docker Compose file contains Sonarr, Radarr, and Bazarr for me. All three use named volumes for their configurations and identical bind-mounted media paths. Since my Jellyfin installation runs natively on Windows, the *arr apps live in Docker while accessing the same media folders.

Getting these working is only half the job, though. With my existing libraries imported, Sonarr and Radarr maintain their respective catalogs. This gives Bazarr a continuously updated picture of everything on your media server. Bazarr takes that information and periodically checks for missing subtitles using your configured providers. When it finds a suitable match, it downloads the file directly alongside the video. Every time Jellyfin scans my library, the subtitle file is already there, and I just select it.

I gave Jellyfin a Kodi makeover, and my media library felt brand-new

My media center has never looked better

2
By  Samarveer Singh

What makes this entire automation even sweeter is that Bazarr doesn't just give up when it can't find a subtitle immediately. It schedules more searches if the initial attempts fail. Furthermore, it also regularly looks for better matches to replace your existing subtitles.

I'll admit there was a little elbow grease involved in getting everything working. However, with everything talking to each other, I've never had to bother with a subtitle-related chore to my routine.

Months later, I haven't had to think about subtitles once

A home-lab automation works best when you forget about it

Every new episode that lands in my library now gets its subtitles automatically, without me having to open a browser, compare release names, or interrupt playback to hunt for an SRT file.

There's one caveat, though. I've pointed Bazarr at OpenSubtitles.com, and its free tier imposes daily download limits. As such, my initial library backfill took a few days. That wasn't really a dealbreaker for me, especially when the alternative is manually downloading subtitles indefinitely. I could also pay for an anti-captcha service and then use it with another subtitle provider for Bazarr, but nothing ever beats free.

I've learned that reliable self-hosting isn't about installing every available integration or provider. Instead, it's more about properly harnessing dependable services to do the tedious work for you.

I stopped choosing between Plex and Jellyfin, and my media server is better because of it

Both Plex and Jellyfin are better when you stop trying to choose between them

19
By  Samarveer Singh

A little automation goes a long way

In the first weeks and months of self-hosting my media server, I loved having complete control over every moving part of the process. Now, however, I've grown to appreciate services that quietly do their job and don't demand my attention every single day.

Of course, no amount of automation can make unreliable subtitle providers disappear overnight, and occasional maintenance is part of the self-hosting bargain. But I'd much rather spend an afternoon getting something working properly than keep repeating the same mundane task for months. My media server has become considerably more enjoyable to use, and that's ultimately what all this tinkering should accomplish.

Docker

Docker Desktop is a one-click-install application for your Mac, Linux, or Windows environment that lets you build, share, and run containerized applications and microservices. It provides a straightforward GUI (Graphical User Interface) that lets you manage your containers, applications, and images directly from your machine.
Docker Desktop reduces the time spent on complex setups so you can focus on writing code. It takes care of port mappings, file system concerns, and other default settings, and is regularly updated with bug fixes and security updates.

item.itunes:title: I tried to find PHP2Shell with a local LLM before it was disclosed, and it almost got there
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
PHP2Shell recently dropped, an RCE vulnerability primarily found using AI tooling, and when its existence first leaked alongside a three-minute demo, I gave my local LLM a shot at trying to find it. PHP's security team had announced that a release fixing two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS 9.2, would arrive the next day at 14:00 UTC, and a video carrying a Calif watemark appeared to show how it could be used to target WordPress, Drupal, phpBB, MediaWiki, and even a basic PHP file. There were no technical details at the time, which made it the perfect test. I wanted to see how far DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, running on a pair of DGX Sparks, could get with only what was public.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Unfortunately, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash didn't find it... but it honestly wasn't too far off, either. At 00:57 UTC, roughly 13 hours before the advisory went up, it hypothesized the right class of bug and tested different versions of that same idea. I had started the test and went off to do something else, so I wasn't too involved in the process at all, as I saw it as an opportune time to see what a local model could do mostly unaccompanied.

Frontier models from the likes of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are significantly better at this, but DeepSeek managed to get quite close. You see, the other reason I felt that was a good test was that my knowledge of PHP's internals are significantly weaker than my knowledge in other web development technologies. I couldn't confidently steer it in any particular direction, and my test of a model's knowledge often involves seeing it work in domains I do understand. DeepSeek had impressed me in that department with a solid track record thusfar, and I wanted to see how that carried into other domains.

DeepSeek actually mentioned the multipart file upload path as its prime suspect at one point, and when it ran a number of tests on it, my own suspicion grew as well. Still, I didn't know enough to keep the model focused on it. What I did learn, though, is that a local model can be useful for this kind of work if you can bring the knowledge and intuition that the model doesn't have.

DeepSeek had a video, a Docker container, and PHP's source code

But not much else

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is a 552B-parameter Mixture of Experts model with an additional 196B Engram parameters that can be streamed from an SSD, and I have it deployed across two DGX Sparks running locally. I used the Pi coding harness and gave the model access to Docker where it could build PHP from source, make debug builds with AddressSanitizer, and test to its hearts content. The only evidence it had to go off of was the CVE, the watermarked video, and PHP's source code on GitHub.

The first 45 minutes started with me telling it that the vulnerability existed, giving it the video to watch, and an instruction to read PHP's source. It took screenshots from the video, noticing that the tool's banner claimed that it worked on every PHP after 5.4.0, the exploit appeared to work against any .php file regardless of the application, and the memory addresses leaked on screen pointed to memory corruption in PHP itself rather than a bug in WordPress or Drupal.

After that, it spent a lot of time focusing on how incoming requests are turned into PHP's superglobals, which turned out to be the right place to look. It never properly identified the vulnerable code, though it twice mentioned session upload progress, which was a feature introduced in PHP 5.4 and enabled by default. It moved on though without making the realization that, as it turned out, those were very much involved in the vulnerabilities.

45 minutes into the session, I provided DeepSeek a rumour that claimed the bug was in PHP's session upload progress handling, which processes multipart uploads before any application code runs. The suggested mechanism was incorrect, though the area of focus was right, and within about half an hour, it had confirmed in the source that this code could start a session from form data while the upload was still being parsed. At the same time, it had also noticed two labels in the video, a "worker strategy" and a number of attempts, and made the conclusion that the exploit relied on state surviving from one request to the next inside the same PHP worker. That turned out to be correct.

Just a few minutes later, it wrote "Memory limit!" in its reasoning, as its hypothesis was that if PHP ran out of memory while an upload was being parsed, the fatal error could interrupt normal cleanup and leave stale state behind. It then proposed triggering that condition and sending a second request to the same worker to see what remained.

The write-up from Wiz showed that the underlying problem was quite similar to what DeepSeek had identified. The problem came from how PHP handled fatal errors, especially out-of-memory errors, as these could interrupt normal cleanup and leave a corrupted internal state behind. A later request could then reuse that stale state, potentially causing memory disclosure or corruption. PHP describes the fix as "Avoid state corruption via bailout." Even though DeepSeek hadn't identified the complete exploit, nor did it identify the specific state that was left, it had described the trigger and the general failure mechanism with minimals clues as to where the problem had come from.

Unfortunately, this is where DeepSeek went off-track. Rather than actually running PHP out of memory, it used an execution timeout to interrupt the request, despite having reasoned a few minutes earlier that timeouts wouldn't fire during that stage of request handling. Its test scripts also had several bugs, including a cleanup command that matched and killed its own shell. After about ten minutes of empty results, it decided the approach was "getting expensive" and moved on.

On other occasions, it came similarly close, and it showed that a crash mid-upload left per-worker state behind, noting in its reasoning that the bug probably "needs bailout+worker state." Hours later, its fuzzing tests killed a PHP worker once in about 700 requests, which it couldn't reproduce and wrote off as luck, but as it turned out, worker churn is one of the warning signs outlined in Wiz's write-up. Those logs are gone so I can't verify if the crash was related as the logs are gone, but someone with knowledge of PHP's internals might stop at that point and ask the model to keep going down that path.

When I shared Wiz's post with the model the next day, it called the root cause "exactly the... pattern I noticed early on but dismissed!"

DeepSeek was better at checking other people's claims than its own

There were a lot of fake PoCs

Between DeepSeek's own tests and the offcial disclosure, plenty of supposed proof-of-concept documents began to circulate, seemingly all generated by different LLMs. There were write-ups, GitHub repos, technical descriptions, and all of them described a use-after-free in the upload-progress code. All of the explanations sounded plausible, often attaching PHP source-code line numbers to back them up.

To test these DeepSeek built a stock PHP 8.4.4, the version one of those PoCs claimed to have been validated on, and ran those circulating exploits against it using both PHP's CGI mode and Apache with mod_php. It then built a second copy with one line removed, deliberately introducing the condition that some PoCs seemingly depended on, as a positive control. Stock PHP got through almost 100 requests just fine, while the modified build suffered 75 worker deaths. DeepSeek also pointed out that one of the repos I'd sent had reached the same conclusion in its own notes, despite also being touted as a PoC for the CVE.

I pushed back on this pretty hard at the time, as DeepSeek kept telling me they weren't real and that what they described wasn't possible, which was right, but my point was that PHP was clearly about to patch two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2. If it wasn't these, it had to be something. DeepSeek did hold its ground while conceding that its results only ruled out those proposed mechanisms rather than the existence of a vulnerability.

Knowing the target is a human's job

An AI can't do everything (yet)

PHP2Shell's credits include Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz, and Calif's Ryan Austin found several paths to remote code execution back at the start of August. Notably, he didn't need use a special AI agent harness or have access to any unavailable models. Instead, he opted to focus on a codebase with a vulnerability history he was familiar with, looking for bugs he suspected were already there.

PHP2Shell's history actually spans two decades, with Calif tracing its lineage all the way back to memory-limit research conducted by Stefan Esser in 2004. On top of that, a 2024 audit by OSTIF and Quarkslab identified a related out-of-memory issue that didn't end up getting fixed as exploitation wasn't actually demonstrated. Austin suspected that other variants of this old bug were still hiding in PHP's codebase, and utilized his LLM to help him find ways to push PHP past its memory limit.

His explanation for why a model wouldn't get there on its own aligns well with what I saw DeepSeek try to do. Austin's primary argument is that that LLMs tend to investigate prominent, recent vulnerabilities and their variants rather looking to obscure, decades-old exploitation techniques. DeepSeek spent a lot of time focused on recent upload progress theories alongside an unserialize bug. Even when it got to the memory-limit idea, it had no particular reason to treat it as anything more than one hypothesis among dozens.

In my case, I've conducted vulnerability research in the past, and have a couple of CVEs to my name. I'd be comfortable scoping out a starter plan for a PHP exploit like this while also catching details like the non-determinstic nature of the bug, but its internals aren't my area of expertise. While I suspected the multipart upload path once I saw the model highlight it, I didn't know enough about PHP's vulnerability history to recognise just how significant that hypothesis from DeepSeek could have been. If I were familiar with Esser's research I'd have pushed more on that, especially given that fatal errors interrupting cleanup and leaving state behind for later requests were a known source of PHP vulnerabilities. Someone else in my position could have insisted that DeepSeek actually trigger an out-of-memory error instead of letting it substitute a timeout.

That's not to say that DeepSeek would have produced a working exploit, as getting from the right class of bug to reliable code execution is a lot of work in its own right, and very few have managed to make it reliable even today. However, identifying a promising hypothesis is useful only if you know when to pursue it, which is where that human expertise could have made the difference.

These are the local models you can use for this

Assuming you have the memory for them

I used DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 for this experiment, but my day-to-day model is GLM-5.3 Flash, a 320B model with 18B active paramaters. This model first appeared as a free model called "Ox Alpha" before being revealed as GLM-5.3 Flash. It's great for tools like ARTEX, an open-source autonomous penetration testing system. ARTEX manages autonomous testing while more dangerous actions can wait on approval, and both the results and some of the approaches I've seen GLM take have been genuinely impressive.

There are smaller options, too, that are more likely to run on the hardware you own. Qwen 3.8 27B is a dense model I've used for reverse engineering, while Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is a 125B-parameter model alongside a 51B N-gram embedding table, with just 6B parameters active per token. These need a very different class of hardware than DeepSeek, and with MoE expert offloading, can run on typical consumer-class GPUs.

There are also a ton of uncensored and cyber-focused models, which are typically community fine-tunes of open models. They're less likely to refuse requests when testing your own systems. It doesn't necessarily make them better at vulnerability research, but it does often let you scale up your testing a lot quicker.

The model is a significant of the equation, but the harness you use matters too. With Pi, DeepSeek had a shell, Docker, and the ability to build and rebuild PHP when it needed to. Most of the useful work came from building real instances of PHP and running tests against it rather than guesswork based on code, and it's what enabled it to disprove the alleged PoCs that were circulating with actual evidence.

Naturally, frontier models still have a major advantage here. Wiz's report says that the company used Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, and models like those, or the likes of Fable or Astra, would likely have needed less steering than DeepSeek did. DeepSeek needed a rumour to focus on the right part of PHP, never reproduced the vulnerability, and never produced a working exploit. It didn't solve PHP2Shell on its own.

Despite that, an open model running on two DGX Sparks identified many of the prerequisites for the exact bug, while being able to categorically disprove the alleged PoCs. If I were someone who was more aware of PHP's vulnerability history, maybe I would have had a pretty good starting point for figuring out what was really going on.

PHP2Shell recently dropped, an RCE vulnerability primarily found using AI tooling, and when its existence first leaked alongside a three-minute demo, I gave my local LLM a shot at trying to find it. PHP's security team had announced that a release fixing two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS 9.2, would arrive the next day at 14:00 UTC, and a video carrying a Calif watemark appeared to show how it could be used to target WordPress, Drupal, phpBB, MediaWiki, and even a basic PHP file. There were no technical details at the time, which made it the perfect test. I wanted to see how far DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, running on a pair of DGX Sparks, could get with only what was public.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Unfortunately, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash didn't find it... but it honestly wasn't too far off, either. At 00:57 UTC, roughly 13 hours before the advisory went up, it hypothesized the right class of bug and tested different versions of that same idea. I had started the test and went off to do something else, so I wasn't too involved in the process at all, as I saw it as an opportune time to see what a local model could do mostly unaccompanied.

Frontier models from the likes of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are significantly better at this, but DeepSeek managed to get quite close. You see, the other reason I felt that was a good test was that my knowledge of PHP's internals are significantly weaker than my knowledge in other web development technologies. I couldn't confidently steer it in any particular direction, and my test of a model's knowledge often involves seeing it work in domains I do understand. DeepSeek had impressed me in that department with a solid track record thusfar, and I wanted to see how that carried into other domains.

DeepSeek actually mentioned the multipart file upload path as its prime suspect at one point, and when it ran a number of tests on it, my own suspicion grew as well. Still, I didn't know enough to keep the model focused on it. What I did learn, though, is that a local model can be useful for this kind of work if you can bring the knowledge and intuition that the model doesn't have.

DeepSeek had a video, a Docker container, and PHP's source code

But not much else

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is a 552B-parameter Mixture of Experts model with an additional 196B Engram parameters that can be streamed from an SSD, and I have it deployed across two DGX Sparks running locally. I used the Pi coding harness and gave the model access to Docker where it could build PHP from source, make debug builds with AddressSanitizer, and test to its hearts content. The only evidence it had to go off of was the CVE, the watermarked video, and PHP's source code on GitHub.

The first 45 minutes started with me telling it that the vulnerability existed, giving it the video to watch, and an instruction to read PHP's source. It took screenshots from the video, noticing that the tool's banner claimed that it worked on every PHP after 5.4.0, the exploit appeared to work against any .php file regardless of the application, and the memory addresses leaked on screen pointed to memory corruption in PHP itself rather than a bug in WordPress or Drupal.

After that, it spent a lot of time focusing on how incoming requests are turned into PHP's superglobals, which turned out to be the right place to look. It never properly identified the vulnerable code, though it twice mentioned session upload progress, which was a feature introduced in PHP 5.4 and enabled by default. It moved on though without making the realization that, as it turned out, those were very much involved in the vulnerabilities.

45 minutes into the session, I provided DeepSeek a rumour that claimed the bug was in PHP's session upload progress handling, which processes multipart uploads before any application code runs. The suggested mechanism was incorrect, though the area of focus was right, and within about half an hour, it had confirmed in the source that this code could start a session from form data while the upload was still being parsed. At the same time, it had also noticed two labels in the video, a "worker strategy" and a number of attempts, and made the conclusion that the exploit relied on state surviving from one request to the next inside the same PHP worker. That turned out to be correct.

Just a few minutes later, it wrote "Memory limit!" in its reasoning, as its hypothesis was that if PHP ran out of memory while an upload was being parsed, the fatal error could interrupt normal cleanup and leave stale state behind. It then proposed triggering that condition and sending a second request to the same worker to see what remained.

The write-up from Wiz showed that the underlying problem was quite similar to what DeepSeek had identified. The problem came from how PHP handled fatal errors, especially out-of-memory errors, as these could interrupt normal cleanup and leave a corrupted internal state behind. A later request could then reuse that stale state, potentially causing memory disclosure or corruption. PHP describes the fix as "Avoid state corruption via bailout." Even though DeepSeek hadn't identified the complete exploit, nor did it identify the specific state that was left, it had described the trigger and the general failure mechanism with minimals clues as to where the problem had come from.

Unfortunately, this is where DeepSeek went off-track. Rather than actually running PHP out of memory, it used an execution timeout to interrupt the request, despite having reasoned a few minutes earlier that timeouts wouldn't fire during that stage of request handling. Its test scripts also had several bugs, including a cleanup command that matched and killed its own shell. After about ten minutes of empty results, it decided the approach was "getting expensive" and moved on.

On other occasions, it came similarly close, and it showed that a crash mid-upload left per-worker state behind, noting in its reasoning that the bug probably "needs bailout+worker state." Hours later, its fuzzing tests killed a PHP worker once in about 700 requests, which it couldn't reproduce and wrote off as luck, but as it turned out, worker churn is one of the warning signs outlined in Wiz's write-up. Those logs are gone so I can't verify if the crash was related as the logs are gone, but someone with knowledge of PHP's internals might stop at that point and ask the model to keep going down that path.

When I shared Wiz's post with the model the next day, it called the root cause "exactly the... pattern I noticed early on but dismissed!"

DeepSeek was better at checking other people's claims than its own

There were a lot of fake PoCs

Between DeepSeek's own tests and the offcial disclosure, plenty of supposed proof-of-concept documents began to circulate, seemingly all generated by different LLMs. There were write-ups, GitHub repos, technical descriptions, and all of them described a use-after-free in the upload-progress code. All of the explanations sounded plausible, often attaching PHP source-code line numbers to back them up.

To test these DeepSeek built a stock PHP 8.4.4, the version one of those PoCs claimed to have been validated on, and ran those circulating exploits against it using both PHP's CGI mode and Apache with mod_php. It then built a second copy with one line removed, deliberately introducing the condition that some PoCs seemingly depended on, as a positive control. Stock PHP got through almost 100 requests just fine, while the modified build suffered 75 worker deaths. DeepSeek also pointed out that one of the repos I'd sent had reached the same conclusion in its own notes, despite also being touted as a PoC for the CVE.

I pushed back on this pretty hard at the time, as DeepSeek kept telling me they weren't real and that what they described wasn't possible, which was right, but my point was that PHP was clearly about to patch two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2. If it wasn't these, it had to be something. DeepSeek did hold its ground while conceding that its results only ruled out those proposed mechanisms rather than the existence of a vulnerability.

Knowing the target is a human's job

An AI can't do everything (yet)

PHP2Shell's credits include Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz, and Calif's Ryan Austin found several paths to remote code execution back at the start of August. Notably, he didn't need use a special AI agent harness or have access to any unavailable models. Instead, he opted to focus on a codebase with a vulnerability history he was familiar with, looking for bugs he suspected were already there.

PHP2Shell's history actually spans two decades, with Calif tracing its lineage all the way back to memory-limit research conducted by Stefan Esser in 2004. On top of that, a 2024 audit by OSTIF and Quarkslab identified a related out-of-memory issue that didn't end up getting fixed as exploitation wasn't actually demonstrated. Austin suspected that other variants of this old bug were still hiding in PHP's codebase, and utilized his LLM to help him find ways to push PHP past its memory limit.

His explanation for why a model wouldn't get there on its own aligns well with what I saw DeepSeek try to do. Austin's primary argument is that that LLMs tend to investigate prominent, recent vulnerabilities and their variants rather looking to obscure, decades-old exploitation techniques. DeepSeek spent a lot of time focused on recent upload progress theories alongside an unserialize bug. Even when it got to the memory-limit idea, it had no particular reason to treat it as anything more than one hypothesis among dozens.

In my case, I've conducted vulnerability research in the past, and have a couple of CVEs to my name. I'd be comfortable scoping out a starter plan for a PHP exploit like this while also catching details like the non-determinstic nature of the bug, but its internals aren't my area of expertise. While I suspected the multipart upload path once I saw the model highlight it, I didn't know enough about PHP's vulnerability history to recognise just how significant that hypothesis from DeepSeek could have been. If I were familiar with Esser's research I'd have pushed more on that, especially given that fatal errors interrupting cleanup and leaving state behind for later requests were a known source of PHP vulnerabilities. Someone else in my position could have insisted that DeepSeek actually trigger an out-of-memory error instead of letting it substitute a timeout.

That's not to say that DeepSeek would have produced a working exploit, as getting from the right class of bug to reliable code execution is a lot of work in its own right, and very few have managed to make it reliable even today. However, identifying a promising hypothesis is useful only if you know when to pursue it, which is where that human expertise could have made the difference.

These are the local models you can use for this

Assuming you have the memory for them

I used DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 for this experiment, but my day-to-day model is GLM-5.3 Flash, a 320B model with 18B active paramaters. This model first appeared as a free model called "Ox Alpha" before being revealed as GLM-5.3 Flash. It's great for tools like ARTEX, an open-source autonomous penetration testing system. ARTEX manages autonomous testing while more dangerous actions can wait on approval, and both the results and some of the approaches I've seen GLM take have been genuinely impressive.

There are smaller options, too, that are more likely to run on the hardware you own. Qwen 3.8 27B is a dense model I've used for reverse engineering, while Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is a 125B-parameter model alongside a 51B N-gram embedding table, with just 6B parameters active per token. These need a very different class of hardware than DeepSeek, and with MoE expert offloading, can run on typical consumer-class GPUs.

There are also a ton of uncensored and cyber-focused models, which are typically community fine-tunes of open models. They're less likely to refuse requests when testing your own systems. It doesn't necessarily make them better at vulnerability research, but it does often let you scale up your testing a lot quicker.

The model is a significant of the equation, but the harness you use matters too. With Pi, DeepSeek had a shell, Docker, and the ability to build and rebuild PHP when it needed to. Most of the useful work came from building real instances of PHP and running tests against it rather than guesswork based on code, and it's what enabled it to disprove the alleged PoCs that were circulating with actual evidence.

Naturally, frontier models still have a major advantage here. Wiz's report says that the company used Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, and models like those, or the likes of Fable or Astra, would likely have needed less steering than DeepSeek did. DeepSeek needed a rumour to focus on the right part of PHP, never reproduced the vulnerability, and never produced a working exploit. It didn't solve PHP2Shell on its own.

Despite that, an open model running on two DGX Sparks identified many of the prerequisites for the exact bug, while being able to categorically disprove the alleged PoCs. If I were someone who was more aware of PHP's vulnerability history, maybe I would have had a pretty good starting point for figuring out what was really going on.

item.title: I started using Power-over-Ethernet in my smart home, and reduced cable clutter wasn’t the only benefit
item.itunes:title: I started using Power-over-Ethernet in my smart home, and reduced cable clutter wasn’t the only benefit
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I bought my first premium network switch, ultra-high speeds between my home lab nodes were the only thing I cared about. But once the initial 10GbE enthusiasm died down, I began looking into other cool features on my networking companion. VLANs, for example, were a killer addition to my smart home-riddled living space, as they helped me protect the rest of my virtualization servers and everyday systems by isolating my insecure IoT gizmos in their own subnet.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Then there’s the Power-over-Ethernet support that my fledgling self completely ignored for the longest time. But once I moved to an independent house, I quickly realized how much of a godsend PoE-compatible switches and devices can be.

I upgraded my home network to prosumer gear - here’s what I learned

This has been an educational experience.

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

My PoE setup cuts down the number of cables I need to run around the house

I don’t have to worry about routing a power cable to my gizmos

Ever since I became a member of the home lab and self-hosting factions, I've begun arming my living space with all sorts of cool gadgets. Take my surveillance camera setup, for example. Since local-only variants tend to retail for dirt-cheap rates, I picked up my fair share of “dumb” cameras and hooked them to my Frigate and Home Assistant servers to get the same object detection features as expensive cloud-based models without the privacy implications of the latter.

Likewise, I’ve decked out my networking setup quite a lot these last couple of months with dummy switches and mesh nodes to ensure the other denizens of my household get proper coverage in every room. Speaking of smart devices, I’ve also got my fair share of smart chimes, LED controllers, and presence-detection units, many of which support hardwired Ethernet connections.

The problem? Since most of these devices require their own power supply and Ethernet cables, I’d have to put up with a lot of wire clutter. Worse still, this includes bulky DC bricks that I can’t just toss into the narrow PETG cable channels I’ve created with my 3D printer.

Now, I wouldn’t go so far as to say that switching to a PoE-heavy setup completely got rid of all wires, as I still need the Ethernet cables to supply both data and power to my devices. However, this neat technology definitely cuts down on the amount of wires running all over the place, because I no longer need an extra set of power cables for each device.

It gives me more flexibility in my WAP and sensor placements

I don’t need to keep them awkwardly near power outlets anymore

Personally, the biggest advantage of Power-over-Ethernet for my smart home is the fact that I don’t need to hunt for power outlets every time I need to plug a couple of devices. Although I had my home lab outfitted with plenty of power sockets around every corner, my living room, attic, and other rooms aren’t as riddled with outlets.

Heck, my porch has a single power socket close to the door, which caused a lot of hassle when I wanted to mount a DIY ring doorbell and sensors, especially since I’d already dedicated said socket to my security camera.

Without PoE, my only option was to rely on power extension cords, which would make my living space resemble a rat’s nest. Not to mention, I’d have to place them at weird angles or risk straining the power cables too much. But now that I’ve got a PoE-heavy setup, I can just use longer Cat6 cables instead of worrying about the short power cables that ship with my devices.

PoE is also pretty easy to use

That said, it does require some precautions

Unlike VLANs and other networking features that I had a bit of a hard time enabling as a beginner, PoE didn’t take any effort to configure. When I connect the PoE-supported ports on my switch to a random gizmo, it sends a low-voltage signal to detect whether the client devices can handle power transmission.

Once it recognizes that the gadget in question supports PoE functionality, it begins supplying power in accordance with the device’s power class. So, pretty much everything is handled by my switch and I don’t need to spend extra time digging through waves of menus within a web UI just to use my devices via PoE.

Of course, PoE still has some ground rules (pun intended) that I need to follow. For example, I typically use copper Cat6 cables instead of cheaper Copper Clad Aluminum wires, as the high electrical resistance on the latter poses a safety hazard for PoE setups.

Likewise, not all devices in my arsenal are PoE-compliant, and I always double-check the voltages on the ones that do support this functionality. My PoE++ switch also grows really hot if I leave it in summer, so I often leave it at the top of my network rack, where it can receive proper airflow.

But PoE is definitely a worthwhile feature for most networking setups

Although I exercise a fair amount of caution when plugging in new devices into the PoE++ ports on my switch, it’s still a neat facility for my home. In fact, if my current switch were to break down, or I ended up upgrading to an even faster networking stack, I’d put PoE at the top of my priority list – right alongside VLAN support – when I go looking for a new switch.

item.itunes:title: I turned an old laptop into a second screen for my PC without needing to take it apart
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you have an old laptop lying around collecting dust, it doesn't have to. You can reuse an old laptop in several ways, but my favorite is repurposing it as a secondary display. For years, I only relied on the built-in display, but once I tried a dedicated monitor, there was no going back. I even got a portable monitor for trips. But an old laptop works perfectly too, sometimes even better, and there are two reasons for that.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

First, it's incredibly simple and anyone, literally anyone, can do it. You don't need any third-party apps or additional hardware. Everything you need is built natively into Windows. And second, this doesn't require any major changes. This means the laptop can serve as a second screen during the day and a reliable streaming solution at night.

A second screen boosts productivity

I have always been a fan of multi-display setups

As I said earlier, when I first tried a multi-monitor setup, I quickly realized what I was missing out on. While a single display isn't all that bad when you have a handful of active programs or tasks to monitor, a second monitor makes multitasking a breeze. For instance, I can have the browser and other critical applications I am actively using on one display, and the ones that don't need as much attention, like the screenshot tool I use for articles, on another. It makes the overall experience so much more streamlined and clutter-free.

For this reason, I have got an external display for almost every situation. There's a dedicated 27-inch monitor on my workstation, a smaller, portable monitor for when I am traveling, and the old laptop that I use occasionally. The only reason it doesn't find as much application is that it's bulkier. But if I hadn't already purchased two external displays, it certainly would have been an integral part of my workflow because it's so easy to set everything up.

You, too, can make this adorable ESP32 1.14-inch desktop monitor

It doesn't need wires, either.

4
By  Simon Batt

It's easier than you think

You don't even need a third-party app

If you ask me, the best part of using your old laptop as a second screen is how easy the setup is, even though everything is wireless. Yes, we won't use an HDMI cable because laptop HDMI ports are designed for output, not input. And we won't be relying on any third-party apps either. Windows has everything you need. Here's some more good news: both systems don't need to be running the same Windows iteration. For example, my old laptop has Windows 10 while my PC runs Windows 11. So, even if your old laptop doesn't support Windows 11, this works well.

As for the setup, open Settings on your old laptop, navigate to System, then into Optional features, search for Wireless Display, tick the checkbox for it, and click Install. Once that's done, go to Projecting to this PC under System settings, and click the Launch the Connect/Wireless Display app to project to this PC option (it may say Connect or Wireless Display, depending on whether your old laptop runs Windows 10 or 11). The screen should show a "ready for you to connect wirelessly message."

On your main computer, open Settings -> System -> Projecting to this PC. Follow the link to install the Wireless Display optional feature, then return to configure projection and open the receiving app. Once your old laptop appears on the list, click the entry, and your system should instantly duplicate the display across both screens.

If you have never tried a multi-display setup, I would recommend switching the projection setting from "Duplicate" to "Extend." This way, you can actually drag apps between displays. Additionally, go to the Display settings and click Identify (or Windows + K) to see how both screens, your PC and the old laptop, are numbered. Once you know that, drag the displays above to rearrange them as you see fit. Personally, I like arranging them the same way the displays are physically present, i.e., if my old laptop is placed to the left of my monitor, that's where it will be in the arrangement.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Adobe's Photoshop has long dominated the graphics editor market, to the point where any signs of artificial edits in photos are called out as being "photoshopped". It wasn't until a few years that a company called Serif entered the market with its Affinity suite, presenting a rival to Photoshop that offered a one-time payment model instead of an expensive subscription, a lot of features, and a user-friendly UI.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But a year ago, everything changed. Affinity went mostly free to use following an acquisition by Canva, and whereas it might have been harder to recommend before, it's now the Photoshop replacement I'd recommend to everyone on Windows or macOS (and soon enough, even Linux).

Free, with some caveats

AI is the selling point

Affinity's big advantage over Photoshop has always been its pricing structure. Prior to adopting its current "freemium" model, Affinity was sold as three separate apps — Photo, Designer, and Publisher — which could be bought individually or as a bundle that would cost around $165 for a lifetime license (outside of sales). At the time, the cheapest Photoshop plan cost $10 per month, so it would only take under a year and a half for Affinity to become the cheaper option. Still, it was a big upfront cost.

Now, Affinity is a unified app and the vast majority of existing features are free to use. Instead, Canva Pro subscribers can get access to a range of AI-powered features from Canva, including things like motion blur reduction, depth estimation, and more. Notably, the basic segmentation model that allows for automated object selection still works with the free version.

Canva does require you to sign in with a free Canva account to use Affinity, but that's a much lower barrier to entry for most people, myself included. And that alone makes it easy to recommend over Photoshop.

This free Photoshop alternative does what GIMP and Krita can't, and I stopped looking after trying it

Lightweight, free, and powerful.

1
By  Parth Shah

It does everything

Including developing RAW photos

I may refer to Affinity as a Photoshop replacement, but in reality, this unified app can do a bit more than simply raster-based image editing. For one thing, it supports vector graphics editing, too, and while I don't often use this to its fullest extent, but it is nice to be able to open an SVG file and rasterize it at whatever resolution I want easily.

More importantly to me, Affinity also includes the ability to load up and develop RAW photos, with almost all of the controls I expect coming from Adobe Lightroom. I can change exposure, brightness, black levels, saturation, and more, along with applying lens corrections with built-in profiles, fixing chromatic aberration, and defringing object edges.

It's true that Lightroom usually does a better job out of the box, and it took me some time to really get the hang of Affinity's controls by hand. But what's great about it is that it lets me create presets, so once I nailed the right look for my photos, I could save those settings and automatically apply them to every photo going forward. A recent update to Affinity also makes it possible to load your last-used settings when opening a RAW file, which makes things even easier.

9 reasons the Affinity creative suite can replace your Adobe subscription

Make the switch from Adobe to Affinity. You'll thank your past self.

11
By  Ruby Helyer

It's great to be able to do all this in a single, free app, because normally, these features require multiple apps. Photoshop does handle RAW files through the included Camera Raw plugin (though I still use Lightroom), but when it comes to other free apps, you're often stuck with tools that aren't really made to play into each other. I'd have to use GIMP for the layer-based editing and Darktable for developing RAW photos, which is just not the best workflow. Affinity makes things much easier.

A user-friendly UI

It's actually easy to understand and use

Perhaps the biggest advantage of Affinity over the many free alternatives to Photoshop, though, is that it's actually usable. I may be exaggerating for comedic purposes there, but I've tried launching GIMP many times in the past, even the version 3.0 that supposedly made things much more user-friendly, and I've simply never been able to get along with its UI.

Especially if you're coming from Photoshop, the interface in GIMP just doesn't quite click. Tools aren't where you'd expect them to be, and icons don't always make it obvious what each one does. One top of that, they may not always behave the way you'd want them to.

Affinity's UI isn't a direct clone of Photoshop, but it definitely feels much more familiar the second you launch it. All the tools are laid out vertically in a side bar, and a small arrow in the corner shows additional options for each one, replicating almost all of there features of Photoshop. The only time I ever really struggled with Affinity was understanding how to use clipping masks, which seem to work differently from Photoshop, but otherwise, things have been smooth sailing.

Tools like GIMP also rely heavily on plugins for features you might expect to be built in, which is where the object selection tool comes in. A lot of the work I do in Affinity or Photoshop is selecting an object from an image and copying it onto a different background, or simply removing the background entirely. Doing this feels impossible in GIMP, and I've heard it can be made much easier with a dedicated plugin, but I simply don't want to have to do that kind of research.

Every time I use free software, I remember why paid options exist

Darktable this, GIMP that — it's not for me

21
By  João Carrasqueira

In Affinity, all I have to do is open the app's settings, install the segmentation model, and it can automatically detect the main subject in most images. Refining the selection is much easier, too, because the selection brush continues to detect colors and edges as you use it, snapping to the edges of objects. It's not as good as Photoshop, it's true, but it's leaps and bounds ahead of any free alternative. And yes, I am familiar with the ArtCraft suite, but I will be discounting vibe-coded clones of proprietary software until it's proven that companies like Adobe don't have legal grounds to take these projects down entirely.

It's not perfect yet

But it's getting there

Affinity is easily the best free Photoshop alternative, but that's not to say it's perfect at everything it does, and in particular, I wish its RAW development tools improved. For one thing, I'd still like to see automatic adjustments as an option, even though saving my last-used presets does make things much easier already. I also prefer how Lightroom offers separate controls for shadows and blacks, as well as highlights and whites. It may sound similar, but it provides a little more granularity that makes it easier to get the perfect result.

More importantly, though, I wish Affinity would provide a dedicated UI that handles RAW photos more smoothly. Right now, it acts more similarly to Photoshop, where any file you open is its own project, and loading up the RAW files as separate projects is just kind slow. I have to limit myself to opening six or so images at a time so it doesn't freeze to the point of crashing on my Mac Mini.

I stopped paying for Lightroom after finding a free open-source editor that handles my RAW files just as well

LightCraft isn't going to be enough for some working professionals, but it's great for the weekend photographer

By  Ty Sherback

With Lightroom, I can browse my files directly and edit them one-by-one without taking so load to load all of them in full-size at once. I can also export multiple JPG files in one go, making it that much easier to edit photos in bulk. It's the main drawback with Affinity for me, but not enough for me to prefer any free alternative over it.

The best Photoshop alternative

Affinity is easily the best replacement for Photoshop, and considering it's free to use, there's no question that it's the way to go. And seeing as it may be getting a proper Linux release soon, it's that much easier to love. If you need an advanced image editing program and don't want to spend money, this is it. Even if you do have money to spend, I would consider exploring this before springing for Photoshop.

Photoshop does handle RAW files through the included Camera Raw plugin (though I still use Lightroom), but when it comes to other free apps, you're often stuck with tools that aren't really made to play into each other. I'd have to use GIMP for the layer-based editing and Darktable for developing RAW photos, which is just not the best workflow. Affinity makes things much easier.

A user-friendly UI

It's actually easy to understand and use

Perhaps the biggest advantage of Affinity over the many free alternatives to Photoshop, though, is that it's actually usable. I may be exaggerating for comedic purposes there, but I've tried launching GIMP many times in the past, even the version 3.0 that supposedly made things much more user-friendly, and I've simply never been able to get along with its UI.

Especially if you're coming from Photoshop, the interface in GIMP just doesn't quite click. Tools aren't where you'd expect them to be, and icons don't always make it obvious what each one does. One top of that, they may not always behave the way you'd want them to.

Affinity's UI isn't a direct clone of Photoshop, but it definitely feels much more familiar the second you launch it. All the tools are laid out vertically in a side bar, and a small arrow in the corner shows additional options for each one, replicating almost all of there features of Photoshop. The only time I ever really struggled with Affinity was understanding how to use clipping masks, which seem to work differently from Photoshop, but otherwise, things have been smooth sailing.

Tools like GIMP also rely heavily on plugins for features you might expect to be built in, which is where the object selection tool comes in. A lot of the work I do in Affinity or Photoshop is selecting an object from an image and copying it onto a different background, or simply removing the background entirely. Doing this feels impossible in GIMP, and I've heard it can be made much easier with a dedicated plugin, but I simply don't want to have to do that kind of research.

Every time I use free software, I remember why paid options exist

Darktable this, GIMP that — it's not for me

21
By  João Carrasqueira

In Affinity, all I have to do is open the app's settings, install the segmentation model, and it can automatically detect the main subject in most images. Refining the selection is much easier, too, because the selection brush continues to detect colors and edges as you use it, snapping to the edges of objects. It's not as good as Photoshop, it's true, but it's leaps and bounds ahead of any free alternative. It may sound similar, but it provides a little more granularity that makes it easier to get the perfect result.

More importantly, though, I wish Affinity would provide a dedicated UI that handles RAW photos more smoothly. Right now, it acts more similarly to Photoshop, where any file you open is its own project, and loading up the RAW files as separate projects is just kind slow. I have to limit myself to opening six or so images at a time so it doesn't freeze to the point of crashing on my Mac Mini.

With Lightroom, I can browse my files directly and edit them one-by-one without taking so load to load all of them in full-size at once. I can also export multiple JPG files in one go, making it that much easier to edit photos in bulk. It's the main drawback with Affinity for me, but not enough for me to prefer any free alternative over it.

The best Photoshop alternative

Affinity is easily the best replacement for Photoshop, and considering it's free to use, there's no question that it's the way to go. And seeing as it may be getting a proper Linux release soon, it's that much easier to love. If you need an advanced image editing program and don't want to spend money, this is it. Even if you do have money to spend, I would consider exploring this before springing for Photoshop.

item.title: I don't need Bambu's 3D scanner, because my phone already scans parts well enough to print replacements
item.itunes:title: I don't need Bambu's 3D scanner, because my phone already scans parts well enough to print replacements
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
3D printing is an immensely enjoyable hobby, but it does have its annoyances. When I need to recreate a physical part without a design file, it can take forever to redesign it. It could be a plastic bracket or just a spacer. The usual process is to measure everything with calipers and build the geometry using CAD. And I'll be honest, I'm not very good at CAD.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The standard recommendation is to buy a handheld 3D scanner. Indeed, I was intrigued by Bambu's upcoming 3D scanner. But there's one more way. This is where phone-based 3D scanning comes in. Instead of building a model from scratch, I can use my phone to capture an existing object and turn it into a 3D model. I've been checking out two apps: Kiri Engine and Polycam. Both these programs use photogrammetry to reconstruct objects from photographs, giving me a simple way to get physical objects into my 3D printing workflow.

My phone turns everyday objects into 3D models

Photogrammetry makes it easy to recreate objects without measuring them manually

The basic idea behind photogrammetry is pretty simple. Instead of measuring a model manually, you can take a series of photographs from different angles. The software then compares overlapping details across the images to determine the object's shape and reconstruct it as a 3D model.

That's useful for all kinds of objects, and especially objects with curves, which can be harder to measure manually. I don't know about you, but I find objects with curved profiles hard to measure effectively with rulers or calipers. Contours, curves, and smaller details are hard to get right. Photogrammetry gives me a much better starting point, since the measurements are largely correct and only need a bit of fine-tuning from me.

I've been using a combination of KIRI Engine and Polycam on my iPhone for this workflow. The apps take photographs of the object, preferably a full 360-degree capture, and turn them into actual 3D geometry that can be exported into other applications.

Polycam usually gets the most recommendations. The object-scanning workflow is simple and adaptable to many use cases, though I tend to stick to object-scanning mode. From there, all you really have to do is position the object in good lighting and move the camera around it while it captures photos. The app then processes these images into a textured 3D model that you can inspect or export. If you subscribe to the paid version, you can upload these images to the cloud for better processing, but I stick to the free version.

Generally, I prefer KIRI Engine to Polycam for ease of use. The basic workflow isn't all that different from Polycam. You're still taking photos of an object to create the model. But KIRI Engine differs with its Featureless Object Scan mode, which I found better at handling objects with reflective surfaces.

I stopped buying dedicated dash cams after realizing my old phone does it better

My old phone can replace a dash cam for free

When capturing photos of an object for a 3D scan, keep a few things in mind. Good light is paramount, and you'll want to capture all aspects of the object. That includes the underside and other areas that the camera can't necessarily see unless you turn the object around.

Of course, scanning is just the first step. Both KIRI Engine and Polycam will let you export your scans in an array of formats, including the obvious ones like STL and OBJ. You'll then want to import these into Blender or your choice of 3D modelling app. In my experience, the generated models are most of the way there, but not fully baked yet. Consider them a starting point.

Photogrammetry produces a mesh, not a parametric CAD design, which means you don't automatically get clean dimensions, properly aligned holes or editable features. A scan can look pretty good while still containing uneven surfaces, stray geometry or inaccuracies that become obvious when I try to fit the printed part.

Similarly, I wouldn't rely on a phone scan for components that need extremely precise tolerances. A replacement bracket might look identical to the original, but a mounting hole that's even slightly misplaced can make the entire print useless. You'll still want to use calipers to measure things like screw spacing and mating surfaces. The advantage is that those measurements let you correct the scan rather than blindly trusting the reconstructed geometry. More importantly, a dedicated 3D scanner tends to have the same limitations.

So, if you're going to correct the model anyway, you might as well start with an app on a phone you already have.

Your phone is a good enough 3D scanner for occassional use

A dedicated 3D scanner has its uses if you are regularly digitizing objects for professional work. But for occasional scans of replacement parts, spending money on dedicated hardware can be hard to justify. It certainly was for me.

Between KIRI Engine and Polycam, you have two great options to make the process more accessible. Even the free version is a good way to capture 3D models with a reasonable degree of accuracy. You'll still need to spend time checking the model and cleaning up meshes, but you don't have to start from scratch.

Beyond the time savings, the biggest advantage is that you're using a tool you already have instead of investing in another device. For occasional use, the results are perfectly reasonable and good enough as an alternative to buying a dedicated scanner.

KIRI Engine

KIRI Engine is a photogrammetry software that runs on the iPhone and uses the camera and LIDAR sensors to create 3D scans.
